## Non-symmetric and general MultiZenoTravel {#sec-nonsymmetric}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Waiting, BĀB̄ situations, and the reduction of general graphs to clique instances
:::

This section relaxes the assumption (S), then the assumption that every central city is joined to
$C_I$ and $C_G$. It corresponds to §5 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md).

### Non-Symmetric Clique MultiZenoTravel {#sec-nonsym}

In this section, we relax the Assumption (S). As a result, the previous method does not work in
the particular case a $(B\bar B)$-pairing is not possible. More precisely, it happens when there
is no choice of cities to perform a $(B\bar B)$-pairing because for two cities $C_i$ and $C_j$
(resp. for $B$ and $\bar B$) we have $d_i < d_j$ and $\bar d_j < \bar d_i$. In such case, the
$(B\bar B)$-pairing on $C_i$ (resp. $C_j$) would increase the duration of the pattern $\bar B$
(resp. $B$) by $2(\bar d_i - \bar d_j)$ (resp. $2(d_j - d_i)$). As a result, without any other
change, the transformed plan has a larger total flight duration for at least one plane which may
result in a larger makespan.

Two regimes must be distinguished. When no flight between central cities is shorter than a detour
through $C_I$ or $C_G$, assumption (A1-NS), the method carries over with durations that depend on
the role of each landing, provided the makespan accounts for the waiting it may force. When such
flights are shorter, plans that move passengers between central cities can do better than the
construction that the 2023 version of this paper proposed for them, through $B\bar A\bar B$
situations.

#### Role configurations {#sec-roles}

A pattern $A$ or $\bar A$ in $C_w$ lasts $d_w + \bar d_w$, a pattern $B$ lasts $2 d_w$ and a
pattern $\bar B$ lasts $2\bar d_w$ (Lemma 3.4(c)). Lists of cities are therefore replaced by role
configurations.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 5.1" >}} **Role configuration.** A role configuration assigns to each plane
$k$ three multisets of central cities, its patterns $B$ ($\mathrm{Dr}_k$, drop-offs), $\bar B$
($\mathrm{Pk}_k$, pick-ups) and $A$ or $\bar A$ ($\mathrm{Cr}_k$, crossings), with
$|\mathrm{Cr}_k|$ odd and the *per-city balance* $\sum_k \mathrm{Dr}_k = \sum_k \mathrm{Pk}_k$.
Its groups are $X_k = \mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k$, its cost is $c(X)$, and the
*role load* of plane $k$ is
$$\lambda_k = 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}_k) + 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk}_k) + \delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k) + \bar\delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k).$$
Passengers are counted through the landings: the configurations for $t$ passengers are those with
$|X| = 2t - p$.
:::

A drop-off and the pick-up of the same passenger form a *link*; with $N$ links, the passengers are
the $N$ linked ones and one per pattern $A$, $(|\mathrm{Cr}_k| + 1)/2$ per plane. Under (S),
$\lambda_k = \ell(X_k)$. Under (A1-NS), every plan gives a role configuration no costlier, whose
role loads are at most its makespan.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 5.4" >}} **Role-load bound.** Assume (A1-NS) and $p \le t$. Every feasible
plan with cost $C$ and makespan $M$ gives a role configuration with $2t - p$ landings, cost at most
$C$ and every $\lambda_k \le M$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Take the scheduled configuration of [Theorem 5.3](#sec-ns-front) and the role
configuration it schedules: its cost is at most $C$, and every role load is a term of its template
value, which is at most $M$ ({{< node "Corollary 5.4" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

The least cost of a role configuration with every $\lambda_k \le T$ is bounded below by a dynamic
program over *imbalance vectors*, the per-city difference between patterns $B$ and $\bar B$ so far
({{< node "Proposition 8.5" >}}), and by two relaxations, which require an odd number of crossings
per plane ({{< node "Proposition 8.3" >}}) or the balance only through Lagrange multipliers
({{< node "Proposition 8.4" >}}).

#### Waiting {#sec-waiting}

If a non-symmetric instance is highly imbalanced in durations, while performing a
$(B\bar B)$-pairing, there is a chance that the plane performing $\bar B$ will have to wait. It
implies that its makespan is not the sum of the durations of its patterns but the moment the
passenger arrives in the central city, plus the remaining duration of its sequence.

Fix an order of the patterns $B$ and of the patterns $\bar B$ of every plane, and a *link
matching*: in each city, which pattern $B$ feeds which pattern $\bar B$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 5.2" >}} **Scheduled configuration, template value.** A *scheduled
configuration* $S$ gives every plane $k$ an ordered list $\mathrm{Dr}_k$ of drop-offs, an ordered
list $\mathrm{Pk}_k$ of pick-ups and a multiset $\mathrm{Cr}_k$ of crossings, and matches every
pick-up to a drop-off. It is *valid* if every $|\mathrm{Cr}_k|$ is odd, every pick-up is matched to
a drop-off in its own city, no two pick-ups to the same drop-off, and there are as many drop-offs
as pick-ups in all; its size, cost and role loads are those of Definition 5.1. Let
$\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) = 2\sum_{j' < j} d_{\mathrm{Dr}_u[j']}$ be the duration of the patterns $B$
that plane $u$ flies before its $j$-th, and
$\mathrm{Suf}_v(l) = 2\sum_{l' > l} \bar d_{\mathrm{Pk}_v[l']}$ that of the patterns $\bar B$ that
plane $v$ flies after its $l$-th. The *template value* of $S$ is
$$M_{\rm tmpl}(S) = \max\Big(\max_k \lambda_k,\ \max_{(u, j;\, v, l) \text{ linked in } C_i}\ \mathrm{Pre}_u(j) + d_i + \bar d_i + \mathrm{Suf}_v(l)\Big).$$
$S$ *schedules* a role configuration if its lists and multisets are that configuration's
drop-offs, pick-ups and crossings.
:::

The *template* of $S$ flies every plane's patterns $B$ in order from time 0, then its patterns $A$
and $\bar A$, then its patterns $\bar B$ in order, every flight departing as soon as possible, a
pattern $\bar B$ leaving its city only once its passenger is there.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 5.5" >}} **Template.** Let $S$ be a valid scheduled configuration with $2t - p$
landings. Then $p \le t$, and for every table of flights between central cities the template of
$S$ is a feasible plan of cost $c(S)$ and makespan exactly $M_{\rm tmpl}(S)$.
:::

A link term is the length of a chain in the template: the plane performing $B$ flies its earlier
patterns $B$ and reaches $C_i$, the passenger then needs $\bar d_i$ to reach $C_G$, and the plane
performing $\bar B$ still flies its later patterns $\bar B$.

One may hope that waiting can always be avoided by choosing the orders and the matching well, so
that the Pareto front would be the Pareto set of (cost, largest role load) over role
configurations. The 2023 version of this paper assumed so, ruling out harmful waiting. It is
false.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 5.7" >}} **Harmful waiting.** Take $n = 2$ cities with $d = (3, 19)$,
$\bar d = (3, 11)$, $c = (5, 1)$, $t = 7$ passengers and $p = 4$ planes, so $2t - p = 10$, with any
flights between central cities satisfying (A1-NS).

*(a)* Some role configuration with 10 landings has cost 14 and every $\lambda_k \le 72$, and every
role configuration with 10 landings and every $\lambda_k \le 73$ costs at least 14.

*(b)* Every valid scheduled configuration with 10 landings and cost below 18 has
$M_{\rm tmpl} > 73$.

*(c)* Every feasible plan of makespan at most 73 costs at least 18.

So some role configuration with 10 landings has cost at most 14 and every $\lambda_k \le 73$, but
no feasible plan has cost at most 14 and makespan at most 73.
:::

Cost 14 means one landing in $C_1$ and nine in $C_2$. In the configuration of (a), three planes
perform an $A$ and a $B$ in $C_2$ (load $30 + 38 = 68$), and the fourth plane $v$ an $A$ in $C_1$
and the three patterns $\bar B$ in $C_2$ (load $6 + 3 \cdot 22 = 72$). In its template, every
passenger left in $C_2$ arrives there at time 19 or later, but $v$ reaches $C_2$ for its first
$\bar B$ at $6 + 11 = 17$. It waits until 19, and its two other patterns $\bar B$ take 44 more: it
finishes at $74 > 72$. By (b) and Lemma 5.5, every template of this configuration ends after 73,
whatever the orders and the matching.

![The instance of Proposition 5.7 (experiment E5). Left: the Pareto front computed with exact waiting (blue) and the two points that only appear when waiting is ignored (orange). Right: the share of random instances on which waiting changes the computed front, for uniform durations and for instances shaped like Proposition 5.7, with 95% Wilson intervals.](figures/e5-harmful_waiting.svg){#fig-waiting .paper-fig}

In the experiment [E5](#sec-e5), random configurations waited harmfully at most 29 times in a
million draws, and waiting changed the computed front of 9 of 150 instances shaped like
Proposition 5.7 and of none of 150 uniform ones.

#### The non-symmetric Pareto front {#sec-ns-front}

A bound on the role loads does not bound the waiting, since it pairs patterns $B$ and $\bar B$ by
counts per city and not along the plan's own hand-offs. The following theorem selects the pairings
along the hand-offs, after removing those that the planes could have avoided.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 5.3" >}} **Schedulable domination.** Assume (A1-NS) and $p \le t$. Every
feasible plan with cost $C$ and makespan $M$ gives a valid scheduled configuration $S$ with
$2t - p$ landings, $c(S) \le C$ and $M_{\rm tmpl}(S) \le M$. The template of $S$ is then a
feasible plan of cost $c(S)$ and makespan $M_{\rm tmpl}(S) \le M$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Replace every flight between central cities by the detour through the hub that (A1-NS)
makes no longer, so that every passenger rides a leg $C_I \to C_x$ and then a leg $C_x \to C_G$
(Lemma 3.2). Then rewire hand-offs by three moves (an *exchange* of the rest of the sequences of
two planes that meet, a *cut* of a zero-time detour into a separate loop, and a *splice* of such a
loop back into a sequence), each of which carries one more passenger through a single pattern,
until every remaining hand-off goes forward in time. The hand-offs then give the links, each link
term is at most $M$, and dropping links or crossings brings the configuration down to $2t - p$
landings ({{< node "Theorem 5.3" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

No order of the flights is used beyond the routes and the chains of the passengers, and zero
durations are allowed.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 5.6" >}} **Non-symmetric front.** Assume (A1-NS) and $p \le t$. Let
$\mathcal K_S$ be the set of the points $(c(S), M_{\rm tmpl}(S))$ of the valid scheduled
configurations $S$ with $2t - p$ landings, and $\mathcal K$ the set of the pairs (cost, least
makespan) of the role configurations with $2t - p$ landings, the *least makespan* of a
configuration being the least $M_{\rm tmpl}(S)$ over the valid $S$ that schedule it. Then
$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K_S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K$, and a list is the Pareto
front of the feasible plans if and only if it is the Pareto front of $\mathcal K_S$.
:::

So under (A1-NS) a constructive algorithm can still focus on plans with $2t - p$ central cities,
with additional care for waiting. ZenoSolver brackets every gap of the front between lower bounds,
the relaxation $L$ of Lemma 3.5 and the bounds of Propositions 8.3 to 8.5, and the templates of the
configurations it builds, which it simulates with their waiting. A gap between consecutive
achieved points $(C_i, M_i)$ and $(C_{i+1}, M_{i+1})$ is closed by an exhaustive search over the
scheduled configurations of cost below $C_i$ whose role loads are at most $M_{i+1} - 1$, the closed
form of Definition 5.2 giving their template values ({{< node "Proposition 8.6" >}}).
Proposition 5.7 shows that the search can be needed: there, the configuration of (a) holds the
bounds of Propositions 8.3 to 8.5 at 14 or below at level 73, while every plan of makespan at most
73 costs at least 18. The experiment [E4](#sec-e4) compares the resulting fronts with exhaustive
searches over all plans.

#### BĀB̄ situations {#sec-short}

Without (A1-NS), a flight between central cities can be shorter than any detour through $C_I$ or
$C_G$. The 2023 version of this paper handled the $B\bar A\bar B$ *situation*, a pattern $B$ in
$C_i$, a *shuttle* $C_G \to C_i \to C_j \to C_I$ carrying the passenger to $C_j$, and a pattern
$\bar B$ in $C_j$, by an augmented instance without flights between central cities (its §2.3 and
§3.3, equations (3) to (6) and Figure 10). Its cities have one duration and one cost per pattern
$A$, $\bar A$, $B$, $\bar B$: a central city $C_i$ keeps $d_i + \bar d_i$, $d_i + \bar d_i$,
$2d_i$, $2\bar d_i$ and the cost $c_i$ for each, and every ordered pair $i \ne j$ adds a virtual
city with durations $\min(d_i + \bar d_i,\ d_j + \bar d_j)$, $\bar d_i + d_{ij} + d_j$, $2d_i$,
$2d_j$ and costs $c_i + c_j$, $c_i + c_j$, $c_i$, $c_j$. A configuration of the augmented instance
gives every plane a number of patterns of each type at every city, with one more $A$ than $\bar A$
per plane, as many $B$ as $\bar B$ at every city, and $t$ passengers, one per $A$ and one per $B$;
its points are its cost, for $2t - p$ landings, with any makespan at least its loads. The phrase "a
$\bar A$ with a null multiplicity" has two readings: the shuttle is not counted, or every $B$ at a
virtual city needs an $\bar A$ there. As printed, the construction misses the front.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 5.10" >}} **The shuttle construction misses the front.** Take $n = 2$,
$d = (1, 3)$, $\bar d = (3, 1)$, $c = (6, 1)$, $t = 3$, $p = 2$, and the flights between central
cities $d_{12} = d_{21} = 2$, $d_{11} = d_{22} = 0$. (AΔ) holds and (A1-NS) fails. The instance has
a feasible plan of cost 15 and makespan 8 (@fig-split), so its front has a point that weakly
dominates $(15, 8)$. In both readings, every configuration of the augmented instance has a plane
whose patterns last at least 10, so every point of the construction has makespan at least 10, and
$(4, 10)$ is one. So the front of the construction is not the front of the instance.
:::

::: {#fig-split}

The plan of makespan 8 of Example 5.10 ($I = C_I$, $G = C_G$; dashed flights are empty).
$p_2$ performs the split crossing $C_I \to C_2 \to C_1 \to C_G$: it leaves $t_3$ in $C_2$ at time 3,
flies empty to $C_1$, and carries $t_1$, left there by $p_1$ at time 1, to $C_G$. $p_1$ takes $t_3$
from $C_2$ at time 7. Both planes finish at 8; the landings are $C_1, C_2, C_2$ and $C_2, C_1$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* The augmented instance has four cities, whose patterns $A$, $\bar A$, $B$, $\bar B$ last
$(4, 4, 2, 6)$, $(4, 4, 6, 2)$, $(4, 8, 2, 6)$ and $(4, 4, 6, 2)$. With 3 passengers on 2 planes,
each plane flies an $A$, which lasts 4, so there is at most one pair of patterns $B$ and $\bar B$.
Without a pair, some plane flies $A\bar A A$, at least 12; with a pair, its $B$ and $\bar B$ last 2
and 6, so the plane flying the longer one reaches at least 10. Both planes crossing at $C_2$, one
of them dropping a passenger there and the other picking it up, gives cost 4 and loads 10 and 6
({{< node "Example 5.10" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

Plane $p_2$ flies a *split crossing*: it leaves a passenger in $C_2$ and takes another from $C_1$,
a link between two cities, which neither role configurations nor the shuttle construction contain.
This is the case of the beginning of this section: $d_1 < d_2$ and $\bar d_2 < \bar d_1$, so no
$(B\bar B)$-pairing within one city is short, as one costs $2 d_x + 2\bar d_x = 8$ in either city.
The split crossing enters at $C_2$, next to $C_G$, and leaves from $C_1$, next to $C_I$; it lets
$p_1$ leave a passenger in $C_1$ and take another from $C_2$ for 2 each, a pairing between two
different cities. For clique instances without (A1-NS), the relaxation $L$ of Lemma 3.5 remains a
lower bound for every plan; a combinatorial description of the front is open
([perspectives](#sec-open)).

### General MultiZenoTravel {#sec-graphs}

We now consider a weighted graph $U = (V, E)$ such that $|V| = n + 2$ and two arbitrary vertices
named $I$ and $G$ (with weight 0), respectively for the initial and the goal cities, not joined by
an edge; every edge has a duration in $\mathbb N$ in each direction, and every other vertex $i$ a
landing cost $c_i$ ({{< node "Definition 5.8" >}}). A MultiZenoTravel instance $\Pi$ is defined by
the triplet $(U, I, G)$; its plans are those of the [model](#sec-plans), with the edges of $U$ as
flights, and $\mathcal F_U$ is its Pareto front. We denote by $\Lambda$ the set of paths over $U$,
and for any path $q$, $|q|$ is the number of cities in the path. We define the functions $\phi$
(resp. $\omega$) as follows:
$$\phi(q) = \sum_{0 \le i < |q| - 1} \mathrm{dur}(q_i, q_{i+1}), \qquad \omega(q) = \sum_{1 \le i < |q|} c_{q_i}.$$
The function $\phi$ provides the duration, while $\omega$ provides the landing cost of the path.
Notice that the first city in a path does not appear in $\omega$ because the initial state is such
that the planes are in the initial city.

The following algorithm $f$ transforms the general MultiZenoTravel transport problem defined by
$(U, I, G)$ into a non-symmetric clique problem:

* For each vertex $i$ find all the simple paths from $I$ to $i$ (resp. from $i$ to $G$) and
  denote this set $\Lambda_{I \to i}$ (resp. $\Lambda_{i \to G}$).
* Construct a new clique instance such that for each
  $(w_i, e_i) \in \Lambda_{I \to i} \times \Lambda_{i \to G}$, there is a city of weight
  $\omega(w_i) + \omega(e_i)$ (the cost of landing in $C_i$ is counted only once) and an edge
  $I \to i$ (resp. $i \to G$) of weight $\phi(w_i)$ (resp. $\phi(e_i)$).
* For all couples of cities $(i, j)$ of the new instance, assign $d_{ij} = +\infty$.

The reduced instance has no flight between central cities. Every city of $f(U)$ stands for one way
of reaching a central vertex and one way of leaving it, and a pattern of $f(U)$ visits one city. A
pattern of $U$, from $I$ or $G$ to $I$ or $G$, may visit several central vertices and hand
passengers over at any of them. The 2023 version of this paper claimed that $U$ and $f(U)$ have the
same Pareto front. This fails, already on a path.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 5.9" >}} **The reduction misses the front.** Let $U$ be the path
$C_I, a, b, C_G$ with durations $1, 2, 1$ in both directions and no other flight,
$c_a = c_b = 1$, $t = 3$ and $p = 2$. Then $f(U)$ has two cities, with
$(d, \bar d, c) = (1, 3, 2)$ and $(3, 1, 2)$, and its front is $\mathcal F_{f(U)} = \{(8, 10)\}$,
as a graph and also as a clique instance for every table of flights between central cities that
satisfies (A1-NS). $U$ has a feasible plan of cost 8 and makespan 8 (@fig-path), so
$(8, 10) \notin \mathcal F_U$ and $\mathcal F_U \ne \mathcal F_{f(U)}$.
:::

::: {#fig-path}

A plan of cost 8 and makespan 8 on the path of Example 5.9 ($I = C_I$, $G = C_G$; dashed flights
are empty). $p_1$ leaves $t_2$ in $b$ at time 3, flies back to $a$, and takes $t_3$ from there at
time 5, all within the single pattern $C_I\,a\,b\,a\,b\,C_G$. Each plane lands twice in $a$ and
twice in $b$, and each traveler changes planes at most once.
:::

In $f(U)$, every role configuration has four landings of cost 2, and a $(B\bar B)$-pairing in
either city puts a load of 10 on one plane. Between the two cities of $f(U)$, a plane passes
through a hub, which takes $\bar d_1 + \bar d_2 = d_1 + d_2 = 4$, twice the edge $a$–$b$. The plan
above does in one pattern what $f(U)$ cannot: leave a passenger at one vertex, fly to the next one,
and take another passenger there. This is the mechanism of the split crossing above.

In conclusion, the reduction of a general instance to a clique instance proposed in the 2023
version of this paper does not preserve the Pareto front (Example 5.9). A characterization of the
front of general instances in the spirit of Corollary 5.6 is open ([perspectives](#sec-open)).
